content: Salmonella was first identified by Daniel E. Salmon, an American veterinarian, in 1884. He isolated Salmonella choleraesuis from pigs suffering from hog cholera. This marked the initial discovery of the bacterium and its association with disease in animals. The classification of Salmonella is based on the Kaufmann-White typing system, which categorizes the bacterium into subtypes based on three antigenic structures: somatic O antigens, surface Vi antigens, and flagellar H antigens. When Salmonella is ingested, the bacteria attach to the intestinal lining using fimbriae or pili. They specifically target specialized epithelial cells, known as M cells, located in the Peyer’s patches of the intestine. The bacteria are internalized through receptor-mediated endocytosis and transported within phagosomes to the lamina propria, where they are released. Once in the lamina propria, Salmonella induces an influx of immune cells. Typhoidal strains attract macrophages, while nontyphoidal strains primarily recruit neutrophils. The Vi antigen of Salmonella typhi plays a critical role in evading the host immune response by preventing antibody-mediated opsonization and complement-mediated lysis. Through the release of cytokines and the migration of mononuclear cells, S. typhi spreads via the reticuloendothelial system, primarily affecting the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Within approximately 14 days, the bacteria enter the bloodstream, leading to secondary metastatic infections such as splenic abscesses or endocarditis. In some cases, the gallbladder becomes infected, resulting in chronic carriage of S. typhi or S. paratyphi, with the bacteria being excreted in bile and subsequently in stool. Nontyphoidal Salmonella infections typically remain localized, while S. typhi and other virulent strains invade deeper tissues through lymphatics and capillaries, eliciting a robust immune response. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) was first described in 1895 by Dr. Connor, a British physician, in identical twin sisters. In 1921, Dr. Johannes Peutz of Holland identified the association between gastrointestinal polyposis and distinctive skin pigmentation. Later, in 1949, Dr. Harold Jeghers in the United States further characterized the syndrome by linking intestinal polyposis and skin pigmentation to the development of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The eponym Peutz-Jeghers syndrome was introduced by A. Bruwer in 1954. In 1998, mutations in the serine/threonine-protein kinase 11 (STK11/LKB1) gene were identified as the genetic basis of the syndrome. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is caused by mutations in the STK11 gene, located on chromosome 19p13.3. The STK11 protein is crucial for second messenger signal transduction, regulating cellular proliferation, maintaining cell polarity, and responding to low-energy states. In mammalian studies, STK11 has been shown to inhibit AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and downstream signaling pathways, including the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). Dysregulation of the mTOR pathway is a hallmark of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Histologically, polyps associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are characterized by a unique smooth muscle core that arborizes throughout the polyp. These polyps can only be definitively identified through histopathological analysis. The prevalence of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is estimated to range from 1 in 8,300 to 1 in 250,000 individuals, with the most likely prevalence being approximately 1 in 100,000. The syndrome typically manifests between the ages of 10 and 30, with an average age of diagnosis of 23 years in males and 26 years in females. Both genders are equally affected. The symptoms of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome often appear in the first decade of life and include hyperpigmentation, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. If left untreated, the syndrome can progress to malignancies such as colon cancer, breast cancer, and other gastrointestinal cancers. Extraintestinal malignancies, including pancreatic, lung, uterine, ovarian, and testicular cancers, are also associated with the syndrome. Complications of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome include intussusception, gastric outlet obstruction, and the presence of extraintestinal polyps. Screening recommendations from the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) include annual physical examinations, complete blood work to assess for iron deficiency anemia, and endoscopic evaluations. The prognosis for Peutz-Jeghers syndrome varies depending on the extent of disease at diagnosis. While the overall prognosis is generally good, the presence of malignancies significantly impacts survival outcomes. Early detection and management are critical in improving long-term outcomes for affected individuals.
